opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't see it as some grand strategy. People sometimes assume that if you want to become a professor, you should stay in your lab, focus on one line of work, and publish as many papers as possible in one direction so you build a clear "brand." I went a different way. I did five internships, and each one was a completely different project in a different environment.

Looking back, I think it was one of the most valuable things I did in my PhD. Each internship was like a short, intense research life. You go somewhere new, you meet new mentors, you see how a different group thinks about problems, what they consider important, and how they work day to day. Some places cared a lot about engineering and scale, others about elegant ideas, others about real product problems. That exposure shaped my taste much more than staying in one comfortable setting would have.

It also forced me to adapt quickly. In three months, you have to figure out a problem, get something working, and make it into a real contribution. That trains a kind of independence and speed that I think matters a lot when you later run your own group. As a faculty member, you're constantly switching contexts, working with students on very different topics, so having practiced that earlier helped.

There was a cost, of course. My research might have looked a bit scattered on paper, and I didn't have one single thread you could easily summarize. But I've come to believe that a faculty position isn't really about having the longest list of papers in one niche. It's about whether you have your own perspective and judgment on what problems are worth working on. The internships gave me collaborators and friends across the field, and more importantly, they helped me form my own view of where research should go. So I don't regret it at all. If anything, I'd encourage students not to be too afraid of exploring.

r001.rationale: He says the internships could make his research look scattered on paper and mentions the conventional advice to build a focused research brand for a faculty career. But he does not clearly state that the internships disadvantaged his own effort to secure a faculty position.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a strategy at all. I think people look back and assume there was a plan, but when I was a PhD student at UCSD I was mostly just curious and, frankly, a little restless. Each summer I'd go somewhere new, Google, Adobe, Microsoft Research, eventually FAIR, and each time the project was almost unrelated to the last one. My advisor Zhuowen Tu was very generous about it. He never said, "You should stay and push one thread." He let me wander.

But looking back, I do think it shaped me in ways that mattered for the faculty path, maybe more than if I had been very focused. A few things.

One is that I learned what good research taste looked like in very different environments. Industry labs and academic labs value different things, and seeing five versions of that calibrates you. You start to recognize when a problem is real versus when it just looks good on a slide. That's hard to learn from a single advisor or a single group, because you absorb one set of biases without noticing.

Two, each project was essentially a mini-PhD in miniature. You arrive, you have twelve weeks, you have to understand the domain, find the gap, execute, and write something up. Doing that five times trains a kind of muscle: how to get up to speed fast, how to decide what to ignore. When you become faculty, that is honestly most of the job. You're constantly entering problems you're not an expert in yet.

Three, and this one I underestimated, it built a network. The people I interned with later became collaborators, coauthors, or just people I could call. When you go on the academic job market, that matters. Letters, visibility, people vouching that you can actually work with others.

Now, the cost. The real cost is that my thesis didn't have a single clean narrative. If you compare it to someone who spent five years on one problem and became the world expert on that one thing, their story on the job market is much tidier. I had to work harder to connect the dots and say, here is the thread, which for me ended up being around network architectures and representation learning, even though the surface topics looked scattered. And there were moments, especially mid-PhD, where I worried I was becoming a jack of all trades.

But I'd push back a bit on the idea that breadth and a faculty position are in tension. The best faculty I know are not the ones who stayed on a single track. They're the ones who had a few different exposures and then, at the right moment, chose to go deep. The internships gave me the breadth; the ResNeXt work and later the ConvNeXt work gave me the depth. I don't think I could have picked the right place to go deep without first seeing the landscape.

So if a student asked me today, I'd say: don't do it as a strategy, do it because you're genuinely curious, and don't apologize for it. Just make sure that at some point you stop sampling and commit. The sampling isn't the problem. Never committing is the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the internships had costs, including a less tidy thesis narrative, but ultimately argues that breadth helped his faculty path and is not inherently in tension with it. It does not state that the five internships were disadvantageous for his faculty-position goal.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tension there. If your goal is to pursue a faculty position, it helps to have a clear research identity—something people associate with you. Doing five internships on five different projects doesn’t necessarily give you that. You spend a lot of time learning a new problem, and the projects may not add up to one obvious story.

But I also think exploration has value. You get to experience different ways of doing research, work with different people, and learn what kinds of problems you actually enjoy. Those experiences can help you develop your own taste, which matters if you eventually want to lead a research group.

So I wouldn’t describe it as the most direct strategy for getting a faculty job. I see it more as an investment in figuring out what kind of researcher I want to be. The important part is eventually turning that breadth into a direction of your own.

r001.rationale: The response says five internships on different projects were not the most direct strategy for getting a faculty job, but it does not say the internships were at five different places or that faculty was his goal at the time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a trade-off. If your goal is very clearly to become a faculty member, doing five internships on five different projects might not be the most direct path. You want to develop a coherent research agenda, and switching projects means spending time learning a new problem and getting started again.

But internships can also help you figure out what you actually want to work on. You get exposed to different problems, different ways of doing research, and different people. Those experiences can eventually inform your own research direction.

So I wouldn’t view the choice only in terms of whether it maximizes your chances of getting a faculty position. The question is whether you’re learning something that matters to you, and whether you can eventually turn those experiences into an independent direction.

r001.rationale: The response says five internships across projects might be less direct for someone aiming to become faculty, but it does not state that this was disadvantageous for Saining given his goal at the time.
